title: Divisibility of $J(C)(k)$ and the $n$-torsion of $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$
statement:
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and let $C/k$ be a smooth proper connected
curve of genus $g$, with Jacobian $J(C)$.

1. For every $n\ge1$, multiplication by $n$ on $J(C)(k)$ is surjective.
2. Let $n>0$. The inclusion $J(C)(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\subset\operatorname{Pic}(C)$
   restricts to an equality
   $$
   J(C)[n](k)=J(C)(k)[n]=\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n],
   $$
   and the degree map induces an isomorphism
   $$
   \operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow[\ \deg\ ]{\sim}\Z/n\Z.
   $$

proof.text: Smoothness and connectedness over the algebraically closed field make the curve geometrically integral and smooth of relative dimension one. The rational-point comparison exists_picardZero_equiv_picardFunctorDegree_zero, together with exists_mulEquiv_of_isPicardZeroMul, identifies Pic^0(C) with the points of the given group-compatible representation of J, as in [sk-thm-picard-main]. Compose the inverse equivalence with the subgroup inclusion to define i. This proves injectivity, its range equality and its displayed characterization by sheafification. By [lem-sc-pic-proper-decomposition], Pic(C) splits as the product of the multiplicatively written integers and a subgroup P0 whose underlying set is Pic^0(C), with first coordinate the degree.

Fix any $n\ge1$. Apply [lem-sc-isogeny-surjective] to the abelian variety $J$ from step 1: for every $y\in J(k)$ there is $x\in J(k)$ with $nx=y$. This proves (1), and in particular $nJ(k)=J(k)$. This lemma requires only $n\ge1$, including when the characteristic divides $n$; its surjectivity is the finite-surjective-fibre argument referred to in the blueprint.

By [sk-def-av-mult-n], $J[n]=J\times_{[n],J,e}\operatorname{Spec}k$. A $k$-point of this fibre product is uniquely a point $a\in J(k)$ satisfying $na=0$, so $J[n](k)=J(k)[n]$. If $L\in\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ satisfies $nL=0$, the degree homomorphism in step 1 gives $n\deg L=0$ in $\mathbf Z$. Since $n>0$, this forces $\deg L=0$. Exactness therefore puts $L$ in $J(k)$, and its same equation says $L\in J(k)[n]$. Conversely, the inclusion of this subgroup into $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ preserves $nL=0$. Hence the inclusion restricts to the asserted equality of torsion subgroups.

source.place: (2), kernel identity and torsion part of the multiplication-by-n diagram

proof.text: Choose the degree-compatible product equivalence of [lem-sc-pic-proper-decomposition]. Compose its first coordinate with integer reduction modulo n, obtaining a homomorphism phi: Pic(C) -> Z/nZ. It is surjective: lift a residue to an integer z and apply the inverse product equivalence to (z,1). Every nth power maps to zero modulo n, since reduction kills n times any residue.

source.place: (2), cokernel part of the multiplication-by-n diagram: induced degree and surjectivity

proof.text: For the reverse kernel inclusion, write the product coordinates of L as (d,y). If phi(L)=0 then d=n*z for some integer z. The subgroup P0 is n-divisible, by transporting the surjectivity from step 2 through the inclusion i and its range equality. Choose M in P0 with M^n=y. Then the inverse product image of (z,M) has nth power L, by injectivity of the product equivalence and its compatibility with powers. Thus the range of the nth-power homomorphism is exactly ker(phi). The first isomorphism theorem gives Pic(C)/nPic(C) isomorphic to Z/nZ. The quotient equivalence sends every class represented by L to phi(L); the first-coordinate formula identifies this value with deg(L) modulo n. The resulting map is degree itself, independent of the auxiliary splitting used to prove its bijectivity.

blueprint_update.statement:
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and let $C/k$ be a smooth proper connected
curve of genus $g$, with Jacobian $J(C)$.

1. For every $n\ge1$, multiplication by $n$ on $J(C)(k)$ is surjective.
2. Let $n>0$. The inclusion $J(C)(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\subset\operatorname{Pic}(C)$
   restricts to an equality
   $$
   J(C)[n](k)=J(C)(k)[n]=\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n],
   $$
   and the degree map induces an isomorphism
   $$
   \operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow[\ \deg\ ]{\sim}\Z/n\Z.
   $$

proof.text: Write $J=J(C)$; it is an abelian variety over $k$ by [sk-thm-picard-main].

*(1)* By [lem-sc-mult-n-isogeny] and [sk-prop-av-isogeny],
$[n]\colon J\to J$ is finite and surjective. Let $y\in J(k)$, viewed as a
closed point $y\colon\Spec k\to J$. The fibre
$F=J\times_{[n],J,y}\Spec k$ is finite over $\Spec k$ because $[n]$ is
finite, and nonempty because $[n]$ is surjective on underlying points and
$y$ lies in the image. So $F=\Spec B$ with $B$ a nonzero finite
$k$-algebra. For a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset B$, the field
$B/\mathfrak m$ is a finite extension of $k$, hence equal to $k$ since $k$
is algebraically closed. The resulting $k$-point of $F$ is a point
$x\in J(k)$ with $[n](x)=y$, that is $nx=y$ in the group $J(k)$. Thus $J(k)$
is divisible ([lem-sc-isogeny-surjective]).

*(2)* The identity $J[n](k)=J(k)[n]$ holds because $J[n](k)$ is the kernel
of $[n]$ on $J(k)$ (universal property of the kernel). By
[sk-thm-picard-main], $J(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$ as groups, and by
[sk-cor-picard-degree] there is an exact sequence of abelian groups
$$
0\longrightarrow J(k)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow{\ \deg\ }\Z\longrightarrow0.
$$
Apply the snake lemma to the endomorphism "multiplication by $n$" of this
sequence. It gives an exact sequence
$$
0\to J(k)[n]\to\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]\to\Z[n]\to J(k)/nJ(k)\to\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow{\deg}\Z/n\Z\to0 .
$$
Here $\Z[n]=0$ since $\Z$ is torsion free, and $J(k)/nJ(k)=0$ by (1).
Hence $J(k)[n]\to\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]$ is an isomorphism, i.e. every
$n$-torsion class in $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ has degree $0$ and lies in
$J(k)[n]$; and $\deg$ induces an isomorphism
$\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\operatorname{Pic}(C)\simeq\Z/n\Z$.
